# Shift handover

What happened this shift and what's still open — a real item log with a current status and an honest flag for what the next shift actually needs to watch.

Family: Daily management · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

A shift handover is what actually gets passed between an outgoing and incoming owner — not a verbal summary that loses detail in translation, but a real item log. Describe what happened and what's open, and a drafted item log names each thing, its current status, and whether it's genuinely time-sensitive enough for the next shift to watch closely.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- Work genuinely spans shifts or owners, and something real can be lost if the handoff is just verbal.
- You want the next owner to know honestly what needs their attention, not everything flagged equally.
- You want a real record of what was open at handoff time, in case something slips later.

Not when:

- There's no real shift boundary — work continues with the same owner, so there's nothing to hand off.
- You'd be flagging every item as needing attention just to be safe — that defeats the point; only genuinely time-sensitive items should be flagged.

## How to fill it in

- **items** — Drafted from your shift description — a real item, its current status, and whether it needs the next shift's attention.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the items actually built.

The example below is the renewal-risk queue's day-to-evening handover on the same day as this catalogue's escalation matrix example. The one flagged item sits right at the edge of that matrix's own Critical escalation trigger — the two artifacts describing the same real moment from two angles.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/shift-handover

## Common mistakes

- **Flagging every item as needing attention.** — If everything is flagged, nothing stands out — the flag only has value when it's reserved for what's genuinely time-sensitive.
- **Writing a status that just restates the item rather than where things actually stand.** — The incoming owner needs to know what's actually happened so far, not just that something exists.
- **Skipping the handover when the shift felt quiet.** — A quiet shift is exactly when a real item can slip through unnoticed — the handover is cheap insurance either way.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **Escalation matrix** — A flagged item's urgency often traces directly to the escalation matrix's own severity definitions and triggers, as in the worked example.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding whether a flagged item genuinely needs attention or can wait
- Deciding how much detail an item's status actually needs

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting specific items, real statuses, and an initial needs-attention flag from a shift description
- Drafting the narrative from the items actually built

Drudgery — automated:

- Counting how many items need attention
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
